title: Network Partitions — They WILL Happen
description: Real examples from AWS, Google, and Cloudflare outages showing that network partitions are inevitable, not theoretical.

segments.text: A network partition is when nodes in your system can't talk to each other, but are still running. It's not a crash. It's worse. Both sides think they're right, and neither can confirm.

Imagine two database replicas can't reach each other. Both accept writes. Both think they're the leader. When the partition heals, you have conflicting data. This is called split-brain, and it's one of the hardest problems in distributed systems.

April 2011. Amazon's US-East region experienced a network partition during a routine configuration change. EBS volumes couldn't replicate. The re-mirroring storm that followed consumed all available capacity. Reddit, Quora, and Foursquare went down for hours.

August 2015. Google lost connectivity to a significant portion of their network for eighteen minutes due to a software bug in their network control plane. Even Google, with the best networking engineers on the planet, can't prevent partitions.
segments.thought_prompt: If Google can't prevent network partitions, what makes you think your system can?

segments.text: July 2020. Cloudflare had a twenty-seven-minute outage caused by a router misconfiguration in a single data center. The bad route propagated via BGP, and suddenly major websites were unreachable worldwide.

What causes partitions? Everything. Router failures, misconfigured firewalls, overloaded switches, submarine cable cuts, software bugs in network stacks, and even squirrels chewing through fiber optic cables. Yes, really.

Here's what makes it worse: partitions can be asymmetric. Node A can send to node B, but B can't send to A. Or partitions can be partial — some messages get through, some don't. This makes detection incredibly difficult.

How do you even detect a partition? You can't distinguish between a slow network and a partitioned network. Is that node dead, or just unreachable? This ambiguity is fundamental and cannot be solved — only managed.
segments.thought_prompt: If you can't tell whether a node is dead or just unreachable, how would you design around that?

segments.text: The key insight is this: don't try to prevent partitions. Design for them. Decide ahead of time what your system should do when nodes can't communicate. Should it stay available or stay consistent?

Strategies include: timeouts with retries, leader leases that expire during partitions, quorum-based voting where a majority must agree, and conflict resolution policies for when partitions heal. We'll explore all of these in later modules.

Remember: network partitions are not edge cases. They are guarantees. The only question is whether your system handles them gracefully or catastrophically. Build for the partition, and everything else becomes easier.
